ClickHouse © is a high-performance relational column-store database to enable big data exploration and 'analytics' scaling to petabytes of data. Methods are provided that enable working with 'Yandex Clickhouse' databases via 'DBI' methods and using 'dplyr'/'dbplyr' idioms.
This R package is a DBI interface for the Yandex Clickhouse database. It provides basic dplyr support by auto-generating SQL-commands using dbplyr and is based on the official C++ Clickhouse Client.

- **Native TCP interface** — this package, `RClickhouse`. It talks to ClickHouse over the native binary protocol (default port `9000`) via the official C++ ClickHouse client. This is *not* the HTTP interface, so connect to the native port (`9000`) rather than the HTTP port (`8123`).
- **HTTP(S) interface** — use `ClickHouseHTTP` (CRAN), a DBI backend built on the ClickHouse HTTP interface (default port `8123`) with HTTPS/SSL support.

- **Arrow Flight SQL interface (experimental)** — an experimental rewrite of `RClickhouse` on top of Arrow Flight SQL is being developed on the `v2-flight-sql` branch. Both the rewrite itself and the Arrow Flight SQL interface are experimental, and Arrow Flight is not exposed by default on ClickHouse Cloud. This branch also provides an HTTP fallback, but it is only a fallback — if you want to use the HTTP interface, prefer `ClickHouseHTTP` (see above).

Comments, reviews, reactions, commit-producing actions, and merges retain your user identity. - **Validating admission webhooks** — admission-time rejection of unsupported mutations (rename, `clusterType` switch, edition/storage changes, replica removal) and cross-field invariants the CRD schema can't express (see Admission Webhooks)

- The operator manages its own AG endpoint certificates — no cert-manager required for the core install (`dist/install.yaml`). cert-manager **is** required only if you deploy via `make deploy` with the validating admission webhooks enabled.
The full annotated sample CR is at `config/samples/sql_v1alpha1_sqlserverinstance.yaml`. Key fields are documented in the API Reference.

The full annotated sample CR is at `config/samples/sql_v1alpha1_sqlserveravailabilitygroup.yaml`. The sample configures a three-replica AG (`clusterType: EXTERNAL`) with two synchronous replicas and one asynchronous replica, LoadBalancer listeners, and SQL Agent enabled. A three-synchronous-replica variant for failover testing is available at `config/samples/sql_v1alpha1_sqlserveravailabilitygroup_3sync.yaml`. Key fields are documented in the API Reference.

On every reconcile the operator runs `EXEC sp_server_diagnostics` directly inside the primary pod via `kubectl exec`. This mirrors the `OpenDBWithHealthCheck` + `QueryDiagnostics` pattern in Microsoft's mssql-server-ha Pacemaker resource agent. It catches SQL Server internal failures that don't immediately crash the process — and therefore don't flip the pod to `NotReady`:
- **If the pod still reports PRIMARY locally** (split-brain after planned failover): issue `ALTER AG OFFLINE` to reset from PRIMARY → RESOLVING.

- **If the pod is in RESOLVING** (unplanned failover): after 15 s, issue `ALTER AG OFFLINE` + bilateral HADR endpoint restart (restart endpoints on both the stuck replica and the current primary). The mirroring transport caches connection state on both sides — restarting only one side is insufficient.

Even with `requiredSynchronizedSecondariesToCommit` left unset (default), a `SynchronousCommit` secondary that has not been definitively marked disconnected keeps the primary waiting on `HADR_SYNC_COMMIT` for its commit acknowledgment — this is SQL Server's own Always On behavior, not something the operator introduces. In testing on AKS, killing the sole secondary during active writes stalled a subsequent write on the primary for several minutes, bounded by how long the operator's NOT SYNCHRONIZING recovery ladder (re-seat → HADR endpoint restart → bilateral restart) took to reconnect it — reads were unaffected until the pending write's schema lock caused other sessions on the same database to stall too. With 3+ replicas this isn't visible because the primary always has another synchronized partner to fall back on.

This mirrors the promote action in Microsoft's mssql-server-ha ag-helper. SQL Server verifies from its local copy of the AG configuration that the target replica had received every committed transaction. If not, it rejects the command with **error 41142** and the operator retries on the next reconcile. `FORCE_FAILOVER_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS` is never used.
|T+0 s|`ALTER AVAILABILITY GROUP FAILOVER` issued on a SYNCHRONIZED secondary|
|T+~1 s|Target secondary atomically becomes PRIMARY; old primary demotes to SECONDARY in-place|
|T+~2 s|Operator detects role change; updates `status.primaryReplica`; listener Service re-points via `ag-role=primary` label|
|T+~10 s|Demoted replica re-establishes database mirroring session with the new primary|
|T+~2 s|Next reconcile detects `NotReady`; `PrimaryNotReadySince` is set; requeue after threshold|
|T+~31 s|`ALTER AVAILABILITY GROUP FAILOVER` issued on target pod|
|T+~32 s|New primary promoted; `status.primaryReplica` updated; listener Service re-pointed|
|T+~60 s|Operator issues `SET (ROLE = SECONDARY)` — may fail with Msg 41104 (stale transport state)|
|T+~75 s|`ALTER AG OFFLINE` + bilateral endpoint restart fires (secondary + primary endpoints cycled)|
|T+~90 s|Transport reconnects; `SET (ROLE = SECONDARY)` succeeds on next reconcile|

**Reconcile time:** on every reconcile the operator compares each replica's PVC size against `spec.storage.dataVolumeSize` and patches `spec.resources.requests.storage` directly on any PVC that is smaller than desired. This is a defense-in-depth check independent of the webhook (which is not enabled by the bundled `dist/install.yaml` — see Admission Webhooks): if the bound StorageClass doesn't support expansion, the operator does not attempt the patch and instead surfaces a `StorageResizing=False` condition with reason `ExpansionUnsupported`. For a `SQLServerAvailabilityGroup`, every replica's PVC is patched — there is no rolling/staged resize; all replicas grow together.
|`True`|`ResizeInProgress`|At least one PVC has been patched to the new size and the CSI driver is (or has just finished) expanding it|
|`False`|`ResizeComplete`|All PVCs are at or above the desired size|
|`False`|`ExpansionUnsupported`|Desired size exceeds at least one PVC's current size, but the bound StorageClass does not support expansion — message explains why|

Most modern CSI drivers (Azure Disk, Portworx, Ceph RBD) support `ExpandInUsePersistentVolumes`: the filesystem grows online with zero pod restarts, as observed with Portworx (`px-csi-mssql`) on AKS — all three AG replicas grew from 20Gi to 25Gi in under 20 seconds with no interruption to the running AG. If your CSI driver instead requires a pod restart to finish the resize (PVC condition `FileSystemResizePending`), restart the pod manually (`kubectl delete pod ...`); for an AG primary, a planned failover first (see Automatic Failover) keeps this a zero-downtime operation.

|`spec.edition`|A SQL Server edition change requires a full reinstall of the binary|
